questions.stem: On the interval a ≤ x ≤ b, f(x) ≥ g(x). The area between the curves y = f(x) and y = g(x) is:
options: the integral from a to b of (f(x) − g(x)) dx
the integral from a to b of (g(x) − f(x)) dx
the integral from a to b of f(x)g(x) dx
the integral from a to b of (f(x) − g(x))² dx
questions.explanation: The area is the integral of the upper function minus the lower function. Integrating g(x) − f(x) gives the negative of the area, because g is the lower curve.

questions.stem: The area of the region enclosed by y = x² and y = x + 2 is:
questions.explanation: The curves meet where x² = x + 2, at x = −1 and x = 2, and the line is above the parabola between them. The area is [x²/2 + 2x − x³/3] from −1 to 2 = 10/3 − (−7/6) = 9/2.

questions.stem: The area between the curve y = sin(2x) and the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = π, is:
questions.explanation: sin(2x) is positive on (0, π/2) and negative on (π/2, π). Each part has area [−cos(2x)/2] over a half, which is 1, so the total area is 2. Integrating straight from 0 to π gives 0, because the signed areas cancel.

questions.stem: The area under y = 1/(1 + x²) from x = 0 to x = 1 is:
questions.explanation: The integral of 1/(1 + x²) is tan⁻¹(x), so the area is tan⁻¹(1) − tan⁻¹(0) = π/4. The value ln 2 would come from treating the integrand as if it were 2x/(1 + x²).

questions.stem: The area under y = 1/x from x = 1 to x = e² is:
questions.explanation: [ln|x|] from 1 to e² = ln(e²) − ln(1) = 2 − 0 = 2. The value 1 − 1/e² comes from integrating 1/x² instead.

questions.stem: The area of the region bounded by y = ln(x), the x-axis and the line x = e is:
questions.explanation: The curve meets the x-axis at x = 1. By parts, ∫ ln(x) dx = x ln(x) − x, so the area is (e − e) − (0 − 1) = 1. The value e − 1 is the width of the interval, not the area.

questions.stem: The area under y = 1/√(4 − x²) from x = −1 to x = 1 is:
questions.explanation: [sin⁻¹(x/2)] from −1 to 1 = sin⁻¹(1/2) − sin⁻¹(−1/2) = π/6 + π/6 = π/3. Stopping at π/6 uses only the part from 0 to 1.

questions.stem: The area under y = 3/((x + 1)(x − 2)) from x = 3 to x = 5 is:
questions.explanation: 3/((x + 1)(x − 2)) = 1/(x − 2) − 1/(x + 1), so the area is [ln((x − 2)/(x + 1))] from 3 to 5 = ln(3/6) − ln(1/4) = ln 2. Multiplying by 3 again, when the partial fractions already include it, gives 3 ln 2.

questions.stem: The area under y = x e^(−x) from x = 0 to x = 1 is:
questions.explanation: By parts with u = x: ∫ x e^(−x) dx = −x e^(−x) − e^(−x). From 0 to 1: (−1/e − 1/e) − (0 − 1) = 1 − 2/e, about 0.264. The value 2/e − 1 is negative, so it cannot be an area.

questions.stem: A solid is formed by rotating the region under y = f(x), for a ≤ x ≤ b, about the x-axis. Its volume is given by:
options: 2π times the integral from a to b of f(x) dx
the integral from a to b of π f(x²) dx
π times the integral from a to b of [f(x)]² dx
π times the integral from a to b of f(x) dx
questions.explanation: Each thin slice is a disc of radius f(x) and area π[f(x)]², so V = π ∫ [f(x)]² dx. Without squaring, the integral gives π times an area, not a volume.

questions.stem: A region between a curve and the y-axis, from y = a to y = b, is rotated about the y-axis. The volume is:
options: π times the integral from a to b of x² dy, with x written in terms of y
π times the integral from a to b of y² dx, with y written in terms of x
π times the integral from a to b of x dy, with x written in terms of y
2π times the integral from a to b of x² dx, with x as the variable
questions.explanation: Slices perpendicular to the y-axis are discs of radius x, so V = π ∫ x² dy, which needs x as a function of y and bounds in y. Integrating y² with respect to x gives rotation about the x-axis instead.

questions.stem: The region under y = √x, from x = 0 to x = 4, is rotated about the x-axis. The volume is:
questions.explanation: V = π ∫ from 0 to 4 of (√x)² dx = π ∫ x dx = π[x²/2] from 0 to 4 = 8π. Integrating √x without squaring gives π × 16/3, which is not a volume.

questions.stem: The line y = x/2, from x = 0 to x = 6, is rotated about the x-axis. The volume of the cone formed is:
questions.explanation: V = π ∫ from 0 to 6 of x²/4 dx = π[x³/12] from 0 to 6 = 18π. This agrees with the cone formula (1/3)πr²h with r = 3 and h = 6.

questions.stem: The semicircle y = √(9 − x²), −3 ≤ x ≤ 3, is rotated about the x-axis. The volume of the sphere formed is:
questions.explanation: V = π ∫ from −3 to 3 of (9 − x²) dx = π[9x − x³/3] from −3 to 3 = π(18 − (−18)) = 36π, which matches (4/3)π(3)³. Integrating from 0 to 3 only gives the hemisphere, 18π.

questions.stem: The region under y = 1/√(1 + x²), from x = 0 to x = 1, is rotated about the x-axis. The volume is:
questions.explanation: V = π ∫ from 0 to 1 of 1/(1 + x²) dx = π[tan⁻¹(x)] from 0 to 1 = π × π/4 = π²/4. Leaving out the π in front of the integral gives π/4.

questions.stem: The region under y = sin(x), from x = 0 to x = π, is rotated about the x-axis. The volume is:
questions.explanation: V = π ∫ from 0 to π of sin²(x) dx = π[x/2 − sin(2x)/4] from 0 to π = π × π/2 = π²/2. The value 2π comes from π ∫ sin(x) dx, without squaring.

questions.stem: The region under y = 2/(x + 1), from x = 0 to x = 1, is rotated about the x-axis. The volume is:
questions.explanation: V = π ∫ from 0 to 1 of 4/(x + 1)² dx = 4π[−1/(x + 1)] from 0 to 1 = 4π(−1/2 + 1) = 2π. The value 4π ln 2 comes from squaring 2 but not (x + 1).

questions.stem: The region bounded by y = x², the y-axis and the line y = 2, with x ≥ 0, is rotated about the y-axis. The volume is:
questions.explanation: With x² = y, V = π ∫ from 0 to 2 of y dy = π[y²/2] from 0 to 2 = 2π. Using x⁴ = y² as the integrand gives 8π/3, which squares the radius twice.

questions.stem: The region bounded by y = 4 − x², the y-axis and the x-axis, with x ≥ 0, is rotated about the y-axis. The volume is:
questions.explanation: Here x² = 4 − y and y runs from 0 to 4, so V = π ∫ from 0 to 4 of (4 − y) dy = π[4y − y²/2] from 0 to 4 = 8π. Integrating 4 alone gives 16π, forgetting the − y.

questions.stem: The region enclosed by y = x and y = x² is rotated about the x-axis. The volume is:
questions.explanation: The curves meet at x = 0 and x = 1, with y = x on top. Using washers, V = π ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x² − x⁴) dx = π(1/3 − 1/5) = 2π/15. Squaring the difference, π ∫ (x − x²)² dx, gives π/30, which is not the washer volume.

questions.stem: The region bounded by y = ln(x), the y-axis, the x-axis and the line y = 1 is rotated about the y-axis. The volume is:
questions.explanation: With x = eʸ, V = π ∫ from 0 to 1 of e^(2y) dy = π[e^(2y)/2] from 0 to 1 = π(e² − 1)/2. The value π(e − 1) uses x instead of x² as the integrand.

questions.stem: When Simpson's rule is used to approximate a definite integral, the number of strips n must be:
questions.explanation: Simpson's rule fits a parabola through each pair of strips, using three points at a time, so the strips must come in pairs and n must be even.

questions.stem: In Simpson's rule with n = 6 strips, the coefficient of f(x₃) inside the square brackets is:
questions.explanation: The pattern of coefficients is 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 1 for x₀ to x₆: odd-numbered points get 4 and interior even-numbered points get 2. x₃ has an odd subscript, so its coefficient is 4.

questions.stem: Using Simpson's rule with n = 2, the integral of x³ from x = 0 to x = 2 is approximated as:
questions.explanation: w = (2 − 0)/2 = 1, so the estimate is (1/3)[f(0) + 4f(1) + f(2)] = (1/3)(0 + 4 + 8) = 4. Leaving out the 1/3 gives 12. Here the estimate equals the exact value, 2⁴/4 = 4.

questions.stem: A function has values f(0) = 1, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 5, f(3) = 10 and f(4) = 17. Simpson's rule with these values estimates the integral of f from x = 0 to x = 4 as:
questions.explanation: With w = 1: (1/3)[1 + 4(2 + 10) + 2(5) + 17] = (1/3)(1 + 48 + 10 + 17) = 76/3. Swapping the coefficients 4 and 2 gives (1/3)(1 + 24 + 20 + 17) = 62/3, and the trapezoidal rule gives 26 instead.

questions.stem: Using Simpson's rule with n = 2, the integral of 1/x from x = 1 to x = 3 is approximated as:
questions.explanation: w = 1, so the estimate is (1/3)[1 + 4(1/2) + 1/3] = (1/3)(10/3) = 10/9, about 1.111. The exact value is ln 3, about 1.099. The trapezoidal rule with the same points gives 7/6, which is less accurate.

questions.stem: Using Simpson's rule with n = 4, the integral of sin(x) from x = 0 to x = π is approximated as:
questions.explanation: w = π/4, so the estimate is (π/12)[0 + 4(sin(π/4) + sin(3π/4)) + 2 sin(π/2) + 0] = (π/12)(4√2 + 2) = π(2√2 + 1)/6, about 2.005. The exact value is 2.

questions.stem: A paddock's width is measured every 10 m along a 40 m boundary, giving widths 0, 12, 16, 14 and 0 metres. Simpson's rule estimates its area, in square metres, as about:
questions.explanation: With w = 10: (10/3)[0 + 4(12 + 14) + 2(16) + 0] = (10/3)(104 + 32) = 1360/3, about 453 m². Swapping the coefficients 4 and 2 gives about 387, the trapezoidal rule gives 420, and using w instead of w/3 gives 1360.

questions.stem: The waiting time T, in minutes, is an exponential random variable with parameter λ = 0.5. The mean of T is:
questions.explanation: For an exponential random variable the mean is 1/λ = 1/0.5 = 2 minutes. The value 0.5 is λ itself, which is a rate per minute, not the mean waiting time.

questions.stem: For an exponential random variable with parameter λ, the standard deviation is:
options: λ, the reciprocal of the mean
questions.explanation: The exponential distribution has mean 1/λ and standard deviation 1/λ, so the two are equal. The variance is 1/λ², which is the square of the standard deviation.

questions.stem: Which is the probability density function of an exponential random variable T with mean 5?
questions.explanation: The mean is 1/λ = 5, so λ = 0.2 and f(t) = λe^(−λt) = 0.2e^(−0.2t). Using λ = 5 gives a mean of 0.2, and without the factor 0.2 the total area would be 5, not 1.

questions.stem: The life T, in hours, of a light globe is exponential with mean 1000 hours. Pr(T > 500) is about:
T is exponential with parameter λ = 0.3. Pr(T ≤ 2) is about:
questions.explanation: Pr(T ≤ t) = ∫ from 0 to t of λe^(−λx) dx = 1 − e^(−λt), so Pr(T ≤ 2) = 1 − e^(−0.6) ≈ 0.451. The value 0.549 is e^(−0.6), the probability that T exceeds 2.

questions.stem: T is exponential with parameter λ = 1. Pr(1 < T < 3) is about:
questions.explanation: Pr(1 < T < 3) = e^(−1) − e^(−3) ≈ 0.368 − 0.050 = 0.318. The value 0.368 is Pr(T > 1), which also includes times beyond 3.

questions.stem: T is exponential with parameter λ = 0.2. The median of T, to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: The median m satisfies e^(−0.2m) = 0.5, so m = ln 2/0.2 = 5 ln 2 ≈ 3.47. The mean is 5, and the median is smaller because the distribution is skewed to the right.

questions.stem: The time T, in minutes, between calls to a help line is exponential with mean 4 minutes. The 90th percentile of T, to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: The 90th percentile q satisfies Pr(T ≤ q) = 0.9, so e^(−q/4) = 0.1 and q = 4 ln 10 ≈ 9.21 minutes. Solving e^(−q/4) = 0.9 gives 0.42 minutes, which is the 10th percentile.

questions.stem: T is exponential with an unknown parameter. Whatever the value of the parameter, the probability that T is greater than its mean is:
questions.explanation: Pr(T > 1/λ) = e^(−λ × 1/λ) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368 for every λ. It is less than 1/2 because the mean is pulled above the median by the long right tail.

questions.stem: T is exponential, and Pr(T > 10) = 0.25. The mean of T, to two decimal places, is:
questions.explanation: e^(−10λ) = 0.25 gives λ = ln 4/10 ≈ 0.139, so the mean is 1/λ = 10/ln 4 ≈ 7.21. The value 0.14 is λ itself, not the mean.
